Minnehaha County in brief

South Dakota's most populous county lies against the Minnesota line, and its seat, Sioux Falls, is the largest city in the state. The Big Sioux River bends south-southeast through the east-central section. Rolling farmland over roughly 814 square miles, dotted with lakes and ponds in the west, fills the county; its name comes from a Sioux word meaning rapid water or waterfall.

Residents numbered 197,214 in 2020. A typical home was valued at $266,600 across 2019 to 2023, and 64 percent of homes have their owners living in them. Besides Sioux Falls, the incorporated places are Baltic, Brandon, Colton, Crooks, Dell Rapids, Garretson, Hartford and Valley Springs.

Health care employs the most people, led by Sanford Health and Avera Health, with the school district, Smithfield Foods, Amazon, Hy-Vee and the big banks behind them. Rentals and inherited houses compete in a metro market. Cash can matter most for a place that needs repairs a conventional lender won't fund.

Where to go and who to call

Four county roles touch a sale. Equalization values the home, the Auditor turns budgets set by elected officials into a tax figure, the Treasurer takes your payment, and the Register of Deeds records the deed.

  • Treasurer: 415 N. Dakota Ave., Sioux Falls, SD 57104. Weekday hours are 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., closed on legal holidays. The phone is (605) 367-4211.
  • Director of Equalization: (605) 367-4228. Covers assessed values and owner-occupied status. Assessments are outside the Treasurer's control.
  • Register of Deeds: 415 N. Dakota Ave., first floor, open 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

Expect crowds at the Treasurer on Mondays, Fridays, the first business day of a month, the last two, and right after a holiday. Schedule a closing-week payment for a calmer day.

Due dates and penalties

Bills are dated January 1. April 30 closes the penalty-free window for half one, and October 31 does the same for half two. Anything still open on May 1 or November 1 is delinquent and picks up a penalty at 10% a year, or .83333% a month.

Mail must carry a postmark of April 30 or October 31 or earlier, while web payments count on the day you make them. For a weekend or holiday deadline, be there by 4:45 p.m. on the final working day; the drop box and the website stay open until midnight. Early payments aren't taken and no discount is given. SDCL 10-21-23 uses the same delinquency dates.

  • By mail, send to 415 N. Dakota Ave., Sioux Falls, SD 57104 with the stub, or else the address, parcel number or bill number. A payment with none of those comes back to you.
  • The drop box sits by the west doors of the County Administration Building and is open at all hours.
  • Web payments add a separate 2.35% convenience fee and may take 7 to 10 business days to post.
  • Delinquent balances are not payable on the website; phone (605) 367-4211.
  • Checks must show a pre-printed in-state name and address.

How a home is valued

Each year November 1 is the legal assessment date, and how the property looks that day determines the next year's assessment. A half-finished house is assessed as half a house. Lots usually go by front footage, acreages by the acre, and buildings by workmanship, size, layout and wear, with a finished basement raising the figure.

Appraisers get a copy of each building permit from a city or the county planning office and review those properties. Routine upkeep, like a new roof or siding, usually doesn't change the assessment. For a rough estimate of a new project's effect, the county suggests taking the cost, labor included, and multiplying by the current tax rate.

Taxable value is set at 85% of full and true value, and every taxing unit finds its levy by dividing the budget gap by taxable value in its area. Homes occupied by their owners are a class of their own. Own and live in the home on November 1; a new owner applies between November 1 and March 15.

Appealing an assessment

Start with a call to the Director of Equalization, who can send an appraiser to review the property. The county also publishes an Appeal Process Guide for formal appeals. A written appeal goes to the local board, which for Sioux Falls residents is the city's Local Board of Equalization, or to the county board.

StepUsual date
Written appeal to local board clerkAround March 13 (postmark counts)
Local board meetsMid to late March
Appeal to county auditorApril 1
County board of equalization sitsApril 8 to 29
Letter to Office of Hearing ExaminersMid May
Circuit court appealWithin 30 days of notice

Check the exact dates with the county, because they shift slightly year to year. Hearings are in the Commission Chambers, third floor, 415 N. Dakota Ave. One dispute can't go to the hearing examiners and circuit court simultaneously.

Timing a sale around the tax calendar

Because the first half is penalty-free only through April 30 and the second through October 31, the month you close changes what you owe. A spring closing may have to clear a half that is days from going delinquent, and the penalty clock of .83333% per month starts the moment a deadline passes. A fall closing faces the same issue with the second half.

Ask the title company who covers each half and write it into the contract. On owner-occupied status, a new owner can apply between November 1 and March 15, and the classification depends on the home being owned and occupied on November 1. Those rules affect what a buyer will pay in tax, so a buyer may ask about them.

What to gather for a closing

Bring the latest tax statement, the parcel number, any permit records for work you did, and the deed. Since appraisers review every building permit, tidy permit history avoids questions about added space. A finished basement counts toward value, so mention it accurately in the listing or offer discussion.

Recording fees

Filing a deed runs $30. On top of that comes the state transfer fee of $1.00 per thousand, the same as $0.50 per $500 of value, set by SDCL 43-4-21 and charged only when the deed involves consideration.

  • Each page beyond 50 costs $2.00 more.
  • Copying is $1.00 a page, and a certification adds $5.00.
  • Plats cost $60, master deeds $75.
  • Federal tax liens and their releases cost $20 each; state tax liens cost nothing to record.

Legal advice is not offered at the Register of Deeds. Let a title company or attorney draft the deed.

Selling with taxes owed

If a tax bill overlaps with a sale, the Treasurer's payoff number drives the settlement statement. Ask for it at (605) 367-4211. Whatever is owed comes out of your proceeds when you close.

Look at the calendar before fixing a closing date. Late April means a first half about to go delinquent; October means the second. We purchase Minnehaha County houses in any condition, tenants and repairs included, and can start from the payoff number.

Frequently asked questions

When are property taxes due in Minnehaha County?

Bills are dated January 1. Half one is penalty-free through April 30 and half two through October 31, and whatever stays unpaid becomes delinquent on May 1 and November 1.

What is the penalty for paying Minnehaha County taxes late?

It is 10% a year, which is .83333% each month. Mail must be postmarked on or before April 30 or October 31 to count as on time.

Who sets my Minnehaha County property value?

Equalization does, and the Treasurer does not. Dial (605) 367-4228 for values, owner-occupied status and appeals. The assessment date by law is November 1.

How much is the South Dakota transfer fee on a home sale?

Fifty cents for each $500 of value, which is $1.00 per $1,000, collected as the deed is recorded. Filing the deed adds $30 in this county.

Can I sell a Minnehaha County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. Get a payoff figure from the Treasurer, and the balance is cleared from your proceeds at closing. Overdue taxes can't be paid on the website, so phone the office.

Pennington County at a glance

Rapid City, the seat and biggest city, anchors this western South Dakota county on the Wyoming border. At 2,784 square miles it ranks third among the state's counties for size. Black Elk Peak, at 7,242 feet, is its high point, and the Cheyenne River and Rapid Creek drain the land. Box Elder, Hill City and New Underwood are the other incorporated places.

The count for 2020 was 109,222, with 116,792 estimated for 2025. The median home value for 2019 to 2023 was $270,400, and half the houses date from 1982 or earlier, meaning aging roofs and furnaces draw comments from inspectors.

Tourism, health care and Ellsworth Air Force Base drive the economy. Military moves and estates put some houses on a hard timeline, and that is the point where owners begin asking about quick sales.

Offices, payment options and fees

Both the Treasurer and Equalization work at 900 Concourse Drive, Rapid City, from 7:00 a.m. until 4:00 p.m. on weekdays. The Treasurer answers at 605-394-2163; Equalization at 605-394-2175.

  • In person: Suite 150. Take cash, a check, a money order, or a debit or credit card.
  • By mail: PO Box 6160, Rapid City, SD 57709-6160, postmarked by the due date.
  • Drop boxes: 130 Kansas City Street and 900 Concourse Drive, available in April and October.
  • Online: current-year taxes only, through Paymentus. No payment over $25,000 is accepted and posting takes 3 to 4 days.

Charges: $1.95 per online e-check, 2% per card, and $40 for any returned payment. Interest and late fees are beyond what the Treasurer or the Board of Commissioners can forgive.

Due dates and what happens when taxes go unpaid

Bills trail by a year: 2023 tax is what gets paid during 2024. Look for the notice around the turn of the year. Half one is delinquent once April 30 passes, half two once October 31 passes, with a weekend deadline pushed to the month's last business day.

The first business day after a deadline starts interest, at the SDCL 54-3-16 rate. Unpaid tax after October 31 puts a tax certificate on the property. Assigning certificates or running a yearly tax sale requires the commissioners' go-ahead, and any sale happens the third Monday of December. SDCL 10-25 lets tax deed proceedings start three years after the certificate sale, and run up to six years after.

  • No installments or payment plans exist for late taxes.
  • Certified funds are required for overdue bills, and the payoff figure comes from the Treasurer.
  • A special assessment must be paid whole before May 1, not in halves.
  • Escrow customers receive a notice for information only; verify that the county received the lender's payment.

Senior freeze and homestead deferral

Older owners have two options, with an April 1 application deadline for each: the elderly and disabled assessment freeze and the homestead deferral. Under SDCL 10-6A the freeze locks assessed value at what it was in the applicant's qualifying year, applying to the house, garage and lot, or one acre if smaller.

Deferral pushes payment of property tax out to the date of sale, charging a reduced interest rate. Anyone who used it needs a payoff from the Treasurer, since the deferred amount is owed when the house sells.

Owner-occupied status is a different matter: it must be your primary residence, only one dwelling in the state qualifies, and the Director of Equalization must have your filing by March 15.

How to appeal your assessment

What an appeal argues: the value is too high, uneven compared with similar homes, or based on bad property data. The amount of tax itself isn't in dispute. Dates are published fresh annually, so check the current set.

StepUsual date
City property: written notice to local board clerk or EqualizationAround March 12
Local board of equalization meetsMid March
Local board decisions mailedLate March
Appeal to county board, or county property noticeAround April 7
County board meetsApril 14 to May 5
County board decisions mailedEarly May
Hearing Examiners, or circuit court within 30 daysMid May

The county's process is to review your notice, talk with Equalization about comparable sales, file the written appeal, schedule an inspection, and then accept or reject the appraiser's recommendation.

Planning a spring or fall closing

The two delinquency dates, May 1 and November 1, give a seller natural checkpoints. Before a spring closing, find out whether the first half has been paid, since delinquent amounts need certified funds and a payoff from the Treasurer. Before a fall closing, do the same for the second half. Special assessments are due in full before May 1, so a spring buyer may want that handled by the seller.

A buyer's title company will also look at whether any tax certificate has been issued on the property. If one has, the process is slower, and a seller should start talking to the Treasurer immediately rather than waiting for the closing date.

Bring a few items to any meeting with the Treasurer or Equalization: the latest notice, a photo ID, your parcel details and, for a freeze or deferral, the paperwork you filed. Staff can tell you quickly what is still open, and a short visit to 900 Concourse Drive can save a week of phone tag. Keep notes on what each office tells you, with names and dates, so your closing agent has the same facts you do. When the sale price is agreed, send the Treasurer's payoff to the title company right away so it can be built into the settlement statement.

Closing a sale

Start with the Treasurer's payoff figure, and let a title company file the deed. SDCL 43-4-21 puts the state transfer fee at $0.50 per $500 of value for deeds with consideration. Recording charges like the $30 per document in SDCL 7-9-15 come from statute, and the Register of Deeds can verify local amounts.

Our company purchases Pennington County houses in present condition, which suits owners facing repairs that cost more than a fast sale would.

Selling with taxes owed

Because tax runs in arrears, what you owe at closing may be for a year you still owned the house. Find out from the Treasurer which half is open and the payoff today. Overdue balances demand certified funds, so arrange a certified check or let the closing agent pay from proceeds.

Used the senior freeze or the homestead deferral? Say so right away, since deferred tax is due at sale and a title company will search for it. For inherited property, confirm who holds the right to sign. Cash skips both the lender and the repair haggling, a plus when time is short.

Frequently asked questions

When are Pennington County property taxes due?

Half one is delinquent after April 30, half two after October 31. The tax runs a year in arrears, with notices mailed near the new year.

Does Pennington County hold a tax sale?

Only with the Board of Commissioners' approval, and then on the third Monday of December. A tax certificate comes first.

Where do I pay Pennington County property tax?

Options are the counter at 900 Concourse Drive, Suite 150, mail to PO Box 6160, a drop box, or the website. The website charges $1.95 per e-check and 2% per card.

What is the Pennington County senior freeze deadline?

April 1, annually, for both the assessment freeze and the homestead deferral, filed with the Treasurer's Office.

Can I sell my Pennington County house with taxes owed?

Yes. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff, and the tax is settled from your proceeds. Late taxes need certified funds, and no payment plans are offered.

Lincoln County in brief

Lincoln County hugs South Dakota's eastern edge, with the Big Sioux River dividing it from Iowa. Gentle hills and farmland fill its 578 square miles, and Canton is the seat. At 65,161 people in 2020 it ranks third in the state, thanks largely to Sioux Falls growing southward.

Median home value ran $323,500 for 2019 to 2023, and owners occupy 72 percent of homes. Beresford, Canton, Harrisburg, Lennox, Sioux Falls, Tea, Worthing, Naomi and Norway Center all lie within or beside the county. A Sioux Falls house on the Lincoln side and a farmhouse by Canton go through the same county offices, yet city and school levies are not the same, so bills can differ a lot between two sellers.

Offices and hours

Three desks share the work. Equalization decides what the property is worth, the Treasurer takes the payment, and the Register of Deeds files the transfer. All sit in the courthouse at 104 N. Main Street, Canton, open weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. apart from holidays.

  • Department of Equalization: Suite 210, 104 North Main Street, Canton, SD 57013, 605-764-2571. Call this office first if your value looks wrong.
  • Treasurer: 104 N. Main Street, Canton, SD 57013, 605-764-5701. Besides collecting property tax and vehicle fees, the staff help people aged 65 or older and disabled residents apply for the freeze and rebate programs.
  • Register of Deeds: files the deed when ownership changes.

Phone lines at the Treasurer open at 9:00 a.m. and close at 4:30 p.m., a shorter window than the counter. A title transfer or new title registration must reach the Treasurer before 4:30 p.m. if it is to be finished the same day.

Due dates and penalties

Property tax comes in halves. April 30 is the deadline for the first, October 31 for the second, and a postmark on either date is accepted. Bills for real estate tax and special assessments go out in January.

SDCL 10-21-23 sets the consequences. Miss April 30 and the first half turns delinquent May 1; miss October 31 and the rest follows on November 1. Interest then starts and recurs on each following first of the month, at the SDCL 54-3-16 rate. Small bills, fifty dollars or less in total, can't be split: the full amount is due April 30. Weekend deadlines move to the final working day of the month.

  • A mailed check takes 5 to 7 business days to be processed.
  • An online payment takes 3 to 5 business days.
  • The online charge is $1.50 per e-check, and 2.4% (never under $1.50) per card or PayPal payment.
  • Late balances can't go through the website, so reach the Treasurer directly.

Sellers should factor in the lag. Money that lands after the deadline can leave interest on your closing statement.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Lincoln County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Valuation and the owner-occupied class

Market value is the starting point, and 85 percent of it becomes the taxable value. Each of the county, the city and the school district divides its budget shortfall by the taxable value inside its borders to produce a levy. Multiply your taxable value by the three levies combined, per thousand dollars, and you have your tax. Schools claim the largest piece.

Equalization appraises land and buildings, looking at how well a building is made, how big and what design it has, what shape it is in, and any extras. Homes you live in can be classed separately. You must live there as your primary residence on November 1, claim only one dwelling in the state, and hand the Certification of Owner-Occupied Dwelling to the county Director of Equalization by March 15.

Contesting your value

Every stage of an appeal carries a firm date. Before anything else, phone Equalization at 605-764-2571, because fixing an error in the property record ends many disputes. If not, write an appeal. Dates shift a little between years, so verify them with the county.

StageUsual date
Assessment notices mailedBy March 1
Owner-occupied filingMarch 15
Written appeal to the local board clerkAround March 13 (postmark counts)
Local board meetsMid to late March
Written appeal to the county auditor, for the county boardApril 1
County board of equalization sitsApril 8 to April 29
Letter to the Office of Hearing ExaminersMid May

Going from the county board to circuit court requires action inside 30 days of service of notice, and you may not run the hearing examiners and circuit court tracks together. Within Sioux Falls, the local board can be reached through the county appeal page or the City Clerk at 605-367-8080, with hearings at Carnegie Town Hall, 235 W. 10th St. Remember the point of an appeal: it says your value is too high or out of line with neighbors. It won't change the rate.

Freeze for seniors and disabled owners

Older and disabled homeowners can apply to freeze their assessment. Each April 1 is the cutoff for turning the application in at the Treasurer's office. As of January 1 you must be 65 or over, or disabled, and total household income, everyone's, has to meet the guidelines. Staff there help with the paperwork.

Frozen values make an old family home inexpensive to hold, and a buyer won't necessarily inherit that bill. Selling a parent's house? Ask the Treasurer if a freeze applied.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Lincoln County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Closing costs and checks

Under SDCL 43-4-21 the transfer fee is $0.50 on each $500 of value, which equals $1.00 per $1,000, and it applies to a deed only when something of value is exchanged. SDCL 7-9-15 sets recording at $30 per document, covering the first 50 pages. Ask the county for today's exact charges.

  • Find out which half-year payment is already made, then set the closing date.
  • A city storm water or maintenance fee may ride the tax roll as its own special assessment.
  • Back taxes become a perpetual lien in South Dakota, which is why title companies demand they be paid or credited at the table.
  • For a delinquent balance, ask the Treasurer for a payoff figure.

If you owe tax and want to sell

Call the Treasurer for the balance, then file the deed with the Register of Deeds. Whatever is unpaid is cleared from your proceeds at closing. A cash buyer can absorb such a balance without a long listing period, which helps if a half is near delinquency.

We purchase houses in any condition around Sioux Falls and throughout Lincoln County, and our written offer gives you a figure to set beside a listing.

How the tax calendar plays against a sale

Think of the year in two big pieces. Notices arrive in January, spring brings the first deadline and the appeal season, and autumn brings the second deadline. A sale that closes in May has to account for a first half that may already be delinquent. A sale that closes in September has to decide who covers the half still ahead. Settle that with the buyer in writing so nobody argues at the table.

Special assessments deserve their own look. A storm water or maintenance charge can ride on the same bill, and a title company will ask about it as well. If the amount is small, it may simply be credited at closing.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What a cash sale skips

A cash purchase doesn't wait for a buyer's loan, an appraisal or a lender's list of repairs. That matters when a half is close to delinquent or when the house needs work no bank will finance. You still need clear title, a recorded deed and a payoff for whatever is owed, but those happen in days instead of weeks. Hold the written offer next to what a listing would net once repairs, carrying costs and showings are counted, and pick the path that fits your calendar.

Before you list

A brief checklist heads off trouble. Find your last tax bill and see which half is still open. Scan it for city special assessments. Check that the owner-occupied certification was filed and whether an elderly or disabled freeze applies. Locate the deed, and settle who can sign for an inherited house.

If the value seems off, call Equalization quickly: appeals run in spring, and a missed date costs you a whole year. Jot down the date and the name of whoever you reach on each call.

Frequently asked questions

When are property taxes due in Lincoln County, SD?

April 30 for the first half, October 31 for the second. Mail it with a postmark on or before those dates to stay interest-free; bills go out in January.

Where do I pay Lincoln County property tax?

Visit the Treasurer at 104 N. Main Street in Canton, or pay by mail or online. Web payments cost $1.50 by e-check or 2.4% by card. Late balances are handled only through the office.

Can I appeal my Lincoln County assessment?

Yes. Call Equalization at 605-764-2571 first. A written appeal then goes to the local or county board of equalization, with state deadlines in March and April.

Is there a tax freeze for seniors in Lincoln County?

Yes, for elderly and disabled owners. You must be 65 or older, or disabled, on January 1, meet the income limits, and apply to the Treasurer by April 1.

Can I sell my Lincoln County house if I owe property tax?

You can. The unpaid amount is settled from your proceeds at closing, so get a payoff from the Treasurer first. A cash sale can close fast around that figure.
